claims.claim: A reader of The Inheritance finds Hobb epic and Lindholm more to the point.
claims.quote: Lindholm writes more to the point

claims.claim: Readers report the books are lived rather than read.
claims.quote: you don't so much read them as live them

claims.claim: Every chapter of Assassin's Apprentice opens with a long epigraph excerpted from an in-world history of the Six Duchies.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver (Campbellsville University), 'History in the Margins: Epigraphs and Negative Space in Robin Hobb's Assassin's Apprentice', Mythlore 41.1 (Fall/Winter 2022) 45-66
claims.quote: Each chapter of the novel begins with a lengthy epigraph

claims.claim: Oliver characterises the register of those in-world history epigraphs as a formal history in a distant, scholarly voice, set against the personal first-person narrative that follows.
claims.quote: largely a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice

claims.claim: Oliver calls the chapter-opening history dry and impersonal, and says the personal main text feels more authoritative and satisfying than it does.
claims.quote: the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter

claims.claim: The chapter-13 epigraph describing Fitz's stepmother Patience carries no sign of the writer's own relationship to her.
claims.quote: contains no hint of the author's relationship to her

claims.claim: In place of personal knowledge the Patience epigraph cites testimony from her nursemaids and publicly available information.
claims.quote: evidentiary quotes from her nursemaids and publicly available information

claims.claim: Oliver names the novel's most striking stylistic element its continual insistence on describing what is not happening.
claims.quote: continual insistence on describing what is not happening

claims.claim: The device Oliver labels 'negative narration' works through sentences that open by saying what a character is not doing or feeling.
claims.quote: sentences that start by telling what a character is not doing

claims.claim: Negative constructions are so frequent in the novel's early chapters that scarcely a page passes without obvious examples.
claims.quote: scarcely a page goes by without obvious examples

claims.claim: Although the frequency of negative constructions falls off later, Oliver says the mode remains one of the book's predominant ones throughout.
claims.quote: remains one of the predominant modes throughout

claims.claim: When Fitz invents a prophetic vision to persuade a duchess, his sentences shift into extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language and parallelism.
claims.quote: extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language, and parallelism

claims.claim: Oliver reads that stylistic shift as marking Fitz's move from a discourse of history into a discourse of fantasy.
claims.quote: Fitz marks his shift from a discourse of history

claims.claim: Late in the novel the epigraphs take on the style of imaginative fiction in place of the style of scholarly discourse.
claims.quote: increasingly infected by the style of imaginative fiction

claims.claim: At the chapter-15 epigraph a poetic lyricism enters the register of the supposedly scholarly history.
claims.quote: a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph

verdicts.trueWording: Hobb writes epic fantasy, Lindholm writes more to the point.
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched with a browser UA (curl, 200). Sentence appears verbatim in the body of the 2011-04 review of The Inheritance: 'this is one of the main differences between Hobb and Lindholm. Hobb writes epic fantasy, Lindholm writes more to the point.' Both limbs (Hobb epic, Lindholm more to the point) on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: you don't so much read them as live them
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched with a browser UA (curl, 200). Opening paragraph, dated 01 August 2015: 'And the trouble with Robin Hobb's books is that you don't so much read them as live them.' Quote verbatim apart from the page's curly apostrophe. The page is one reader (Jackie Morris), but the generalized second person 'you' carries the claim's plural 'Readers'.

verdicts.trueWording: Each chapter of the novel begins with a lengthy epigraph selected from a history of the kingdom, the Six Duchies
verdicts.note: Wayback raw PDF capture 20240707045408id_ (live dc.swosu.edu viewcontent.cgi returns 403 Cloudflare even with browser UA, referer and landing cookies); text extracted with pypdf. Quote verbatim on journal p.45 (PDF p.4), matching the cited page. Every limb supported: 'Each chapter', 'lengthy epigraph', 'selected from a history of the kingdom, the Six Duchies, also written by Fitz' (in-world).

verdicts.trueWording: largely a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice
verdicts.note: Wayback raw PDF capture 20240707045408id_ (live dc.swosu.edu viewcontent.cgi returns 403 Cloudflare even with browser UA, referer and landing cookies); text extracted with pypdf. Verbatim on p.45: 'The chapter epigraphs are excerpts from a public document, largely a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice. The main narrative, on the other hand, is undefined, perhaps a private text or even an internal monologue, filled with Fitz's reminiscences instead of "objective" history.' The 'first-person' limb is carried by the article's own abstract: 'before giving a first-person personal narrative'.

verdicts.trueWording: feels more authoritative and satisfying than the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter
verdicts.note: Wayback raw PDF capture 20240707045408id_ (live dc.swosu.edu viewcontent.cgi returns 403 Cloudflare even with browser UA, referer and landing cookies); text extracted with pypdf. Verbatim on p.57 (PDF p.16), matching the cited page: 'The "marginalia" here (that is, the main text) feels more authoritative and satisfying than the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter, as it allows the reader to more fully imagine her.' Both limbs on the page; note Oliver adds 'but objective', and makes the assessment at the chapter-13 instance.

verdicts.trueWording: This lengthy excerpt contains no hint of the author's relationship to her
verdicts.note: Wayback raw PDF capture 20240707045408id_ (live dc.swosu.edu viewcontent.cgi returns 403 Cloudflare even with browser UA, referer and landing cookies); text extracted with pypdf. Verbatim on p.56 (PDF p.15), matching the cited page: 'Chapter 13, for instance, opens with an epigraph describing his father's widow, Patience. This lengthy excerpt contains no hint of the author's relationship to her or that any information in it came from his experience of her.' Oliver's wording is 'his father's widow' rather than 'stepmother' — the same relation, entailed by the page.

verdicts.trueWording: particularly extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language, and parallelism
verdicts.note: Wayback raw PDF capture 20240707045408id_ (live dc.swosu.edu viewcontent.cgi returns 403 Cloudflare even with browser UA, referer and landing cookies); text extracted with pypdf. Verbatim on p.59 (PDF p.18), matching the cited page: 'a shift in style as Fitz narrates his "dream." His description employs several syntactic patterns typical of the elevated style associated with fantasy novels, particularly extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language, and parallelism.' The persuasion limb is supported on the same page — 'he convinces her ... by claiming he has had a prophetic dream, "a vision"' — and the addressee is a duchess ('she was no longer a common girl, but a duchess').

verdicts.trueWording: here a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph
verdicts.note: Wayback raw PDF capture 20240707045408id_ (live dc.swosu.edu viewcontent.cgi returns 403 Cloudflare even with browser UA, referer and landing cookies); text extracted with pypdf. Verbatim on p.62, matching the cited page: 'the best example ... occurs at the start of the "misted" section in chapter 15, which begins with an epigraph describing the experience of using the Skill ... whereas in the earlier epigraphs Fitz has largely kept the style of the epigraphs and the main text separate, here a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph.' The 'supposedly scholarly history' limb is the article's standing characterisation of the epigraphs (p.45).
